title: She Finished Seventh in the Trials. They Still Could Not Leave Her Out.
excerpt: Double Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker will lead India's 30-member shooting squad at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya — but her selection as a double starter tells a story about depth, politics, and pragmatism.
body:
The National Rifle Association of India announced its 30-member shooting contingent for the 2026 Asian Games on Thursday, and the name at the top of the list was the one everyone expected — and the one that almost was not there.

Manu Bhaker, India's double Olympic medallist from Paris 2024, finished seventh in the women's 10m air pistol selection rankings after the Stage 4 trials in Dehradun. By the NRAI's own selection criteria, that result should have shut the door. It did not.

## The Double-Starter Loophole

The Asian Games organisers imposed a hard cap of 30 athletes on India's shooting delegation — a sharp constraint for a country that fields competitive squads across rifle, pistol, and shotgun disciplines. With 36 event slots to fill, the NRAI needed athletes who could compete in multiple events. Bhaker, whose 25m pistol form has been strong, was selected as a "double starter" alongside Esha Singh, Rudrankksh Balasaheb Patil, and Vidarsa K. Vinod.

The logic is sound. Bhaker's 25m pistol credentials are beyond question — she finished second in the trials, behind only Esha Singh, who has been in devastating form all year and won the Munich World Cup earlier this season. As a double starter, Bhaker fills two event slots with one roster spot. The math works.

But it also means that shooters who outranked her in the 10m air pistol trials — including world champion Samrat Rana and Olympic bronze medallist Sarabjot Singh, who both failed to crack the top three — have been left behind. The selection committee's mandate was to maximise medal potential, not to reward trial rankings. In Indian shooting, as in Indian cricket, the committee always has the final word.

## The Squad in Full

The 30-member contingent is balanced across disciplines:

**Rifle:** Parth Mane, Himanshu Dhillon, Rudrankksh Patil, Elavenil Valarivan, Sonam Maskar, Vidarsha Vinod, Aishwary Tomar, Niraj Kumar, Tilottma Sen, Ashi Chouksey

**Pistol:** Suruchi Singh, Esha Singh, Manu Bhaker, Anish Bhanwala, Rahi Sarnobat, Kedarling Uchaganve, Gaurav, Kamaljeet

**Shotgun:** Kynan Chenai, Ahyvar Rizvi, Shapath Bhardawaj, Neeru, Manisha Keer, Aashima Ahlawat, Anantjeet Gill, Bhavtegh Gill, Mairaz Khan, Parinaaz Dhaniwal, Raiza Dhillon, Maheshwari Chauhan

The mixed team pairings are particularly interesting. Suruchi Singh Phogat and Kedarling Uchaganve will represent India in the 10m air pistol mixed team, while Elavenil Valarivan and Parth Mane pair up in the 10m air rifle mixed team — both combinations based purely on trial performance.

## Esha Singh: The Quiet Contender

If there is a shooter in this squad whose form screams gold medal favourite, it is Esha Singh. The 21-year-old from Hyderabad topped the 25m pistol trials, won the Munich World Cup, and has been consistently among the top three in international competitions throughout 2026. She will enter Aichi-Nagoya as the shooter India expects most from — a pressure that Bhaker, with her Olympic pedigree, can absorb but that few others have tested against.

Veteran Rahi Sarnobat, the 2018 Asian Games gold medallist, adds experience to the pistol squad. At 33, this is almost certainly her last major multi-sport event. Her presence alongside the 24-year-old Bhaker and the 21-year-old Singh represents three generations of Indian women's shooting — a depth unimaginable a decade ago.

## The Aichi-Nagoya Venue

The shooting events will run from September 17 to October 3 at the Aichi Prefectural General Shooting Range. The Asian Games themselves span September 19 to October 4. For NRIs in North America, the time difference means early morning viewing — a rhythm that Indian sports fans have grown accustomed to from years of watching cricket in England and Australia.

## Why the Diaspora Should Care

India's shooting programme is one of the country's genuine medal factories at multi-sport events. At the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou, India won 22 shooting medals, including seven golds. The sport has produced household names — Abhinav Bindra, Manu Bhaker, Saurabh Chaudhary — that resonate with the diaspora in ways that track and field or wrestling rarely do.

The Aichi-Nagoya squad is the strongest India has sent to an Asian Games. But it is also a squad shaped by compromise, by the hard arithmetic of roster caps, and by the inescapable reality that in Indian shooting, a seventh-place trial finish does not mean what it should — not when your name is Manu Bhaker.

NRAI President Kalikesh Singh Deo put it plainly: "Selecting this team was a challenging task given the exceptional depth and quality of talent in Indian shooting today."

He was not wrong. The depth is real. The quality is undeniable. And the politics, as always, are part of the package.
